transcript.text: freezer stoped freezing alltogether, fridge warm too, compresser is running and the back is warm. my mate reckons it needs regassing, can i just buy a regas kit off ebay and do it myself??

Short answer: no, and it probably wouldn't help anyway. And there's a decent chance it doesn't need gas at all.

## Why a DIY regas is a bad idea

• Most eBay "regas kits" are for car air con (R134a or R1234yf). Most modern fridges use R600a (isobutane), so the gas would be wrong.
• R600a is flammable. It's basically lighter gas, and handling it inside a kitchen without proper gear is genuinely risky.
• Fridges are sealed systems. They don't "use up" gas. If it's low, there's a leak, and topping up without finding and fixing the leak just means it'll be empty again soon. A fix means brazing, pulling a vacuum, and weighing in an exact charge. That needs specialist tools.
• It's likely illegal. In the UK, EU, and Australia, handling refrigerants requires certification (F-gas rules in the UK/EU, an ARCtick licence in Australia).

## What's more likely wrong

Your symptoms (compressor running, back warm, freezer AND fridge both warm) often point to a frost-free/defrost fault, especially if it's a fridge-freezer where the fridge gets its cold air from the freezer. The cooling coil behind the freezer's back panel ices up solid, airflow stops, and everything warms up. A warm back actually suggests the system is still shifting heat, which argues against it being out of gas.

Things to check:

1. Look for heavy frost or ice on the freezer's back panel, or a solid block of ice behind it if you can remove the panel.
2. Listen for the fan in the freezer when the compressor's running. With the door open, you may need to press the door switch to make it run. No fan means a likely culprit.
3. Try a manual defrost: empty it, unplug it, and leave the doors open for 24–48 hours with towels down. Plug it back in.
• If it works fine for a week or two and then fails again, it's almost certainly the defrost system (heater, thermostat/sensor, or timer/control board). Those are cheap parts, often £10–40, and very DIY-able.
• If it still doesn't get cold after a full defrost, then a leak or compressor fault becomes more likely.
4. Check the basics: clean the condenser coils at the back or underneath, make sure there's airflow space around it, and check the door seals.

## If it does turn out to be a gas leak

Get a proper fridge engineer to diagnose it. Leak repair plus regas usually runs a few hundred quid. On a fridge more than about 8–10 years old, that's often more than it's worth, so replacing it may make more sense.

If you tell me the make and model, I can help you figure out where the defrost parts are and what's commonly failed on it.

its an indesit, about 9 yrs old. no frost anywhere, freezer back wall isnt even cold, and i can hear the fan going. the back is only barely warm now tho. plate says R600a on it. i did chip ice out the freezer with a knife a few months back if that matters

That detail matters a lot. Unfortunately it changes my guess.

## What's probably happened

Your new info points to lost refrigerant, and the knife is the most likely cause:

• No frost anywhere and the freezer wall isn't even cool. If there were gas in the system, you'd get at least some cold or frost somewhere.
• The fan is running, so it's not an airflow or defrost fault.
• The back is only barely warm now. The condenser has little heat to get rid of because there's little or no refrigerant circulating.
• You chipped ice out with a knife. This is one of the most common ways fridge-freezers die. The refrigerant pipes often run just under the surface of the freezer walls, base or shelves, and one small nick is enough. Sometimes the leak is slow, which fits it failing a few months later rather than straight away.

To check, look where you were chipping for:

• a small hole, dent or scratch through the surface
• an oily mark (refrigerant carries a bit of compressor oil)
• a faint hiss, though by now it's probably already empty

## Safety note

R600a is flammable, but the charge in a domestic fridge is tiny, usually 30–80g. If it's leaked over weeks or months, it's long gone. If you ever hear active hissing, open a window and avoid flames or sparks nearby. Otherwise, no need to worry.

## Can it be fixed?

Technically yes, but it's rarely worth it on a 9-year-old Indesit:

• A fridge engineer would need to repair the pipe (sometimes impossible if it's foamed into the cabinet), pull a vacuum and recharge with R600a. Expect £150–300+, often with no guarantee.
• The kitchen-grade epoxy "freezer repair kits" only seal the hole. They don't put the gas back, so on their own they won't fix it.
• A comparable new fridge-freezer is roughly £300–450, more efficient, and comes with a warranty.

## What I'd do

1. Check your home insurance. Some policies cover accidental damage or loss of frozen food. It's worth a quick look.
2. If you want certainty, get a fridge engineer to diagnose it (often £50–80 call-out). Most will tell you straight away whether a repair makes sense.
3. Realistically, budget for a replacement. Many retailers will take the old one away when they deliver the new one. It has to go to proper recycling because of the refrigerant and insulation foam.

For the next one, defrost by switching off and using a bowl of hot water and a plastic scraper, never anything sharp.
